Gift-card bonus value: compare the percentage, the redemption plan and the cash-price alternative

Convert a hypothetical bonus into two clearly defined percentages, track remaining restricted credit, and compare upfront card funding with cash paid for the same purchases over time.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare an invented store-credit bonus with planned use and a cash-price alternative

Interactive planning lab

Purchases deducted from card by the horizon$88
Restricted credit still held at the horizon$22
Upfront cash paid less cash for the same purchases so far$16.4

Original hypothetical merchant gift-credit arrangement, not a current offer. Cash paid loads equal paid credit plus the entered bonus. Paid and bonus credit form one assumed noncash pool, with no expiry, fees or restrictions on the selected basket during the modeled horizon; actual paid and promotional balances may have different terms. Use is entered as a plan, not a forecast or probability, and occurs uniformly at each month-end. Basket amounts are comparable total checkout amounts; tax is not calculated separately. The alternative pays cash for exactly the same purchases when they occur at the selected lower total price. Prices stay fixed, and no interest, discounting, reward points or extra unplanned purchases are assumed. Remaining credit stays visible and is not written off, refunded or assigned a terminal cash value. The cash-outlay difference is therefore not an overall investment return, saving rate or realized loss. Positive means more cash has been committed to the card than the matched purchases have so far required elsewhere; negative means less.

The central idea

A bonus percentage needs a denominator and a use plan. Compare the same basket at its available cash price, while keeping unspent credit separate from both bank cash and a realized loss.

01

Identify the cash payment and the restricted credit it buys

A merchant bonus can add purchasing credit without adding money to a bank account. Before evaluating the percentage, record how much cash must be paid, how much credit is loaded, where it can be used and which planned purchases will actually use it.

The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s gift-card guide explains how purchases reduce a card balance and why its terms matter. This tool assumes a merchant-only credit pool, rather than a payment-network card or an account from which cash can be withdrawn. It does not determine the legal rules for a particular card.

The default pays CAD 100 at month zero and receives CAD 10 of additional credit, producing CAD 110 of loaded value. Paid and bonus amounts are combined under identical assumed use conditions during the chosen horizon. A real promotion may give its paid balance and bonus different restrictions or dates, so that combined-pool assumption must be checked separately.

02

Convert a bonus on cash paid into a discount on goods received

The bonus is CAD 10 divided by CAD 100 paid, or 10%. If all CAD 110 is used on goods that otherwise cost the same CAD 110 in cash, the saving as a share of that basket is CAD 10 divided by CAD 110, or about 9.09%.

Those two percentages describe the same arrangement with different denominators. The first measures added credit relative to the upfront payment. The second measures the conditional discount on the full amount of purchases. A percentage cannot be transferred between the two bases without conversion.

The percentage chart isolates this calculation by assuming full use and identical checkout prices. It does not claim the selected partial-use case has earned a 9.09% return. Nor does it incorporate the competing cash price entered elsewhere in the tool. Separating that simple denominator question makes it easier to see what the headline bonus actually measures.

03

Unspent credit remains visible instead of being treated as a loss

The selected use plan redeems 80% of the loaded CAD 110 by the horizon, or CAD 88. Restricted credit of CAD 22 remains. The waterfall reconciles the paid credit, bonus and purchases deducted without pretending that the bonus arrived as another bank deposit.

The alternative checkout price is assumed to be 5% lower for exactly the same purchases. Those purchases would therefore have cost CAD 83.60 elsewhere. The card required CAD 100 of cash upfront, which is CAD 16.40 more cash committed than those matched purchases have required so far.

That difference is not a CAD 16.40 realized loss. The cardholder still owns CAD 22 of unused restricted credit under the model. No expiry, write-off, cash refund or terminal cash valuation is applied to that remainder. The cash comparison answers a narrower question about money already paid, and it must be read alongside the remaining balance.

04

A cheaper cash-price alternative can absorb part of the bonus advantage

Now consider full use of the default CAD 110, with the same 5% lower competing checkout price. The complete basket would cost CAD 104.50 elsewhere. Paying CAD 100 for the card would save CAD 4.50 in cash on those same purchases, rather than CAD 10.

Relative to the CAD 104.50 alternative, that saving is about 4.31%. The difference comes from comparing an actual assumed basket price instead of using the card’s face amount as the only baseline. No merchant prices or available deals have been collected; the 5% difference is an authored input.

The comparison requires comparable total checkout amounts. If one price omits tax, delivery, fees or a required additional purchase, it needs adjustment before entering the calculation. The model also assumes the goods are already part of the household’s plan. Buying extra items only to consume credit changes the basket and does not establish that the bonus has improved the budget.

05

Track when cash leaves, rather than reading credit as a bank reserve

The cash chart pays the entire card amount at month zero. The matched alternative pays only as the selected purchases occur, uniformly at each assumed month-end. Both paths acquire the same basket quantities over that horizon, but commit bank cash on different dates.

The lines show cumulative cash paid, not bank balances or net wealth. Money committed to the merchant is not assumed available for another bill just because it still appears as credit on the card. The unspent balance also cannot be assigned to two future shopping plans at once.

The illustration excludes any interest or other use of cash retained outside the card. It likewise assumes fixed prices, no fees and no expiry during the selected period. These are modeling conditions, rather than statements that actual promotional credit has no restrictions. Timing and terms can matter even when full redemption would produce a favorable nominal cash comparison.

06

Use the grid to test a plan without predicting future redemption

The matrix changes both the credit-use fraction and the competing price difference. A positive cell means more cash has been paid to the card than the matched purchases have required elsewhere by that point. A negative cell means less. Remaining credit is excluded from this outlay measure while staying owned, so the colors are not final profit or loss estimates.

With the default bonus and 5% competing price difference, about 95.69% of loaded credit must be used before the matched alternative’s cumulative cash spending reaches the original CAD 100 card payment. That is a cash-commitment threshold, not an economic break-even valuation of the unused balance or a recommendation to shop more.

A sufficiently cheaper alternative can remove even the full-use cash advantage. For example, if the same CAD 110 basket costs 15% less elsewhere, its cash price is CAD 93.50, below the card’s CAD 100 cost even after every credit is used. Evaluate the percentage, the intended basket and the timing together, and keep the remaining restricted balance visible throughout.
